specPoints.text: understand how to carry out calculations involving gas volumes and the molar volume of a gas (24 dm3 and 24 000 cm3 at room temperature and pressure (rtp))

primer.text: Moles from mass and moles from solution working are both in hand; gases now take the same treatment. At room conditions every mole of gas fills the same 24 dm3, so a weighed mass of gas converts straight into a volume.

lessons.title: Avogadro's Law and the Molar Gas Volume
lessons.opening: One mole of any gas fills the same space at room temperature and pressure: 24 dm3, or 24,000 cm3. That molar gas volume turns any gas volume into moles and back again, whatever the gas is.
keyPoints: At room temperature and pressure one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm3, or 24,000 cm3.
RTP means 20 degrees Celsius and one atmosphere of pressure.
Avogadro's law: equal amounts of gases at the same conditions occupy the same volume.
Moles of gas equal volume divided by molar volume; volume equals moles times molar volume.
Divide by 24,000 instead of 24 whenever the volume is given in cm3.

low.restatement: At 20 degrees and one atmosphere, every mole of gas occupies 24 dm3 whatever its identity; 24,000 cm3 is the same figure in smaller units. Moles = volume / 24; volume = moles x 24.
low.analogy: Identical suitcases hold identical clothes counts regardless of brand: one mole fills 24 dm3 whether hydrogen or carbon dioxide, so the gas's name never enters the sum.
low.examPointer: Table style: 3 mol of hydrogen gives (3 x 24) = 72 dm3; 1,200 cm3 of oxygen gives (1,200 / 24,000) = 0.05 mol - match the divisor to the unit.

medium.restatement: The molar gas volume is a property of the conditions, not the gas: RTP fixes 24 dm3 per mole, so amounts of any gases compare by volume alone. The triangle hides nothing deeper - cover moles, volume or 24 and read the step.
medium.analogy: A standard pallet always holds the same box count whatever the goods; counting pallets counts boxes. Counting 24 dm3 units counts moles, whichever gas stacks them.
medium.examPointer: Quoting RTP as 20 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere earns the mark; 0 degrees belongs to a different temperature's version of the value.

check.stem: What is the molar gas volume at RTP?

options.explanation: One mole of any gas occupies 24 dm3 at room temperature and pressure, equal to 24,000 cm3.
The figure is 24 dm3; 24 cm3 is a thousand times too small.
The cm3 figure is 24,000; one zero has been lost here.
22.4 dm3 belongs to 0-degree conditions, not the 20-degree RTP of this specification.
Room temperature and pressure is fixed at 20 degrees Celsius and 1 atm for these sums.
0 degrees is not room temperature in this specification; RTP is 20.
25 degrees feels room-like but the specification pins 20.
The pressure half of RTP is 1 atm, not 2.

check.stem: What is the amount, in moles, of methane in 225.6 dm3 at RTP?

options.explanation: Moles = volume / 24, so 225.6 / 24 = 9.4.
225.6 x 24 travels the triangle backwards; the molar volume divides.
Dividing by 24,000 fits cm3 data; this volume is already in dm3.
options.misconception: cm3 divisor used on dm3 data

options.explanation: 24 / 225.6 answers the reverse question; the gas volume divides by the molar volume.

check.stem: 0.25 mol of carbon dioxide at RTP has what volume, in cm3?

options.explanation: Volume = moles x molar volume; in cm3 the molar volume is 24,000, so 0.25 x 24,000 = 6,000.
0.25 x 24 gives 6 dm3; quoting it as cm3 shrinks it a thousand-fold.
options.misconception: dm3 molar volume used on a cm3 question

options.explanation: 0.25 / 24,000 answers the reverse question; volumes come from multiplying.
24,000 / 0.25 flips the triangle; the moles multiply the molar volume.

options.text: Equal amounts of gases at the same temperature and pressure occupy the same volume
options.explanation: The law compares amounts and volumes directly; gas identity plays no part.

options.text: Equal masses of gases occupy the same volume at RTP
options.explanation: The law counts moles, not grams; equal masses of different gases hold different mole counts.

options.text: Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of atoms
options.explanation: The law counts molecules; diatomic and triatomic gases break any atom-based version.
options.misconception: atoms counted where molecules are meant

options.text: All gases occupy 24 dm3 regardless of amount
options.explanation: 24 dm3 is the volume of one mole; the volume scales with the amount present.

lessons.title: Finding Gas Volumes from Mass and Equations
sourceHeadings: Using mass to calculate the volume of a gas
lessons.opening: Gas volumes do the reacting-mass trick without any Mr at all: under Avogadro's law the coefficients of the equation already are the volume ratio. Masses still convert through moles first, and the units the question names decide whether 24 or 24,000 does the dividing.
keyPoints: Convert a gas mass to moles with Mr, then multiply moles by 24 for the volume.
Coefficients in the balanced equation give the ratio of gas volumes directly under Avogadro's law.
One volume of propane needs five volumes of oxygen when the coefficient ratio is 1 : 5.
Total product volume adds the product coefficients first, then scales the given volume.
Use the units the question asks for; 24 pairs with dm3 and 24,000 with cm3.

low.restatement: A mass of gas crosses to moles through Mr, then multiplies by 24 for its volume; 154 g of nitrogen does 154 / 28 = 5.5 moles and 5.5 x 24 = 132 dm3.
low.analogy: Posting parcels: weigh a box, divide by the weight of one standard box to count boxes, multiply by the space each pallet slot takes. Grams to moles to volume is the same three-beat rhythm.
low.examPointer: The 154 g nitrogen question is two marks per step: Mr first, moles second, and only then does 24 appear.

medium.restatement: Reacting gas volumes skip Mr entirely: under Avogadro's law the coefficient ratio is the volume ratio, so 150 cm3 of propane demands five times its volume of oxygen. Total product volume adds the product coefficients first, then scales.
medium.analogy: Dance partners: the equation pairs one propane with five oxygen molecules, and volumes pair identically - 150 cm3 of one needs 750 cm3 of the other, no weighing needed.
medium.examPointer: Reacting-volume answers must quote the units the question used: 750 cm3 and 1,050 cm3 in cm3, not a surprise switch to dm3.

check.stem: What volume does 88 g of carbon dioxide occupy at RTP? (Mr of CO2 = 44)

options.explanation: 88 / 44 = 2 moles, and 2 x 24 = 48 dm3.
88 g is two moles, not one; each mole fills its own 24 dm3.
88 x 24 skips the moles step; grams are not moles.
options.misconception: mass multiplied straight into the molar volume

options.explanation: 44 / 88 = 0.5 answers the reverse; 88 g divides by 44 to give 2 moles.

check.stem: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O. What volume of oxygen reacts with 150 cm3 of propane, both measured at RTP?

options.explanation: The coefficients pair 1 propane with 5 oxygen, and volumes follow the same ratio: 5 x 150 = 750.
150 / 5 shrinks the volume; propane is the smaller side and oxygen the larger.
Equating the volumes ignores the balancing 5 in front of the oxygen.
5 x 150 = 750; nothing in the equation supplies another factor of ten.

check.stem: In the same combustion, what is the total volume of the gaseous products from 150 cm3 of propane?

options.explanation: The products carry 3 + 4 = 7 ratio units, and 7 x 150 = 1,050.
Only the water's 4 was used; the carbon dioxide's 3 must join it.
Only the carbon dioxide's 3 was used; the water's 4 completes the total.
7 x 24 uses the dm3 molar volume on a cm3 question; volumes scale by the ratio, not by 24.
options.misconception: molar volume applied to cm3 data

check.stem: Why do reacting gas-volume questions need no relative formula masses?

options.text: Under Avogadro's law the coefficients already give the ratio of gas volumes
options.explanation: Equal moles of gas fill equal volumes, so the equation's proportions transfer straight to volumes.

options.text: Because all gases have the same relative formula mass
options.explanation: Gases have different formula masses; volume equality comes from mole equality, not mass equality.

options.text: Because gas masses are always conserved
options.explanation: Mass conservation balances the equation; it does not convert volumes.
options.misconception: conservation invoked for the wrong job

options.text: Because volumes are measured in dm3
options.explanation: The unit choice is convention; the shortcut comes from the law itself.

check.stem: What is the amount, in moles, of oxygen in 1,200 cm3 at RTP?

options.explanation: In cm3 the molar volume is 24,000, so 1,200 / 24,000 = 0.05.
1,200 / 24 belongs to dm3 volumes; cm3 data needs 24,000.
options.misconception: dm3 divisor used on cm3 data

options.explanation: 24,000 / 1,200 flips the triangle; the gas volume divides by the molar volume.
1,200 x 24,000 inflates; the molar volume divides the volume.

glossary.definition: The counting unit for amount of substance; one mole of any gas fills 24 dm3 at RTP.
Equal amounts of gases at the same temperature and pressure occupy the same volume.
The volume occupied by one mole of any gas: 24 dm3 or 24,000 cm3 at RTP.
Room temperature and pressure: 20 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere.
The balancing number in front of a formula in an equation.
A symbol equation whose atom counts match on both sides; its coefficients set gas-volume ratios.
Burning a fuel in oxygen, as in the propane example of this note.

workedExample.prompt: What is the volume of 154 g of nitrogen gas at RTP? (N 14)
